newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy admits delay in tackling jobs problem.
newsitem.headline: Italy admits delay in tackling jobs problem.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who put employment at the top of his agenda when he took office 10 months ago, has been slow to get to grips with Italy's jobless problem, a senior member of his coalition said on Thursday.
"We must be honest," Cesare Salvi, leader of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) in the Senate (upper house), said in a radio interview. "On the jobs problems, the government is late."
The PDS is the biggest party in the centre-left government.

Prodi said two weeks ago employment rose 0.4 percent in 1996 and he expected a clear improvement in 1997, but the most recent data showed unemployment at 12.2 percent in October with the jobless problem especially acute in the underdeveloped south.

Union leaders are planning a mass rally for jobs later this month and Pietro Larizza, whose UIL trades union confederation is one of Italy's big three labour groups, warned on Thursday they would call a general strike if more was not done.
President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro has summoned Prodi and other ministers to the presidential palace for a meeting later on Thursday to thrash out what he called the "terrible" situation.

Prodi's government signed a pact for jobs with unions and employers last September, including a reduction in the working week, incentives for people starting their own businesses and tax breaks on research, to try to boost the employment market.

He said at the time the pact would have an immediate impact on jobs. Since then, however, his room for manoeuvre has been greatly narrowed by a huge austerity budget and he plans to unveil another mini-budget in the coming weeks in a bid to join a European single currency at its planned 1999 launch.
Salvi, speaking to private station Italia Radio, noted that a draft bill on the jobs pact was not presented in the Senate until January and full details still had to be worked out.
He said the "demagogic and hardly reasonable" attitude of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, whose support gives Prodi a parliamentary majority, had not helped matters.
"But it is not fair to dump all responsibility onto that party," Salvi said.
He said the PDS wanted the same energy and determination that had been shown in Italy's drive to clean up its unruly public finances to be applied to the jobless problem.
"We know that the problems are very complex, that there are no miracle cures...but we also know that the question of employment is an absolute priority," Salvi said.
Larizza, in an interview with La Stampa, said if the government did not show "concrete action" before the planned rally in Rome on March 22, "the unions would move into open conflict".
He added: "We would have no other weapon at hand than recourse to a general strike."
Union leaders are due to meet on Saturday in the southern city of Reggio Calabria to plan the rally, which they say will attract hundreds of thousands of people.
